title: Static electricity and sparks
keyIdea: Rubbing two materials together moves electrons from one to the other. It does not make charge. The material that gains electrons becomes negative; the one that loses them is left positive. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, across a gap. A charged object can even pull on neutral paper by pushing its electrons to one side. When enough charge builds up, it can jump a small gap as a spark: a shock from a door handle, or lightning on a huge scale.
familyTip: On a dry day, rub a balloon on a wool jumper and hold it near torn-up tissue paper, then near a thin stream of tap water. Ask which way the electrons moved and why the water bends towards the balloon. Then hang two rubbed balloons on threads and watch them push apart.

visual.caption: Attract or repel? Drag each pair, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: rub electrons onto a balloon, decide attract or repel, lift neutral paper, make a spark at a door handle and sort insulators from conductors.

kid: Everything is made of atoms. Atoms hold positive charges in the middle and negative electrons around the outside. Most things have the same amount of each, so they are neutral.

When you rub a balloon on a wool jumper, some electrons move from the jumper onto the balloon. Only the electrons move. The balloon now has extra electrons, so it is negative. The jumper has lost some, so it is left positive. No charge was made; it just moved.

Charges push and pull without touching. Like charges repel: two negative balloons push apart. Unlike charges attract: the balloon and the jumper pull together. A charged balloon can also lift neutral paper. It pushes the paper's electrons away, so the near side is left positive and is pulled up.

Charge can build up on you when you shuffle on a carpet. When your hand gets close to a metal handle, the extra electrons jump the gap as a spark, and you feel a small shock. Lightning is the same thing on a huge scale. Plastic, glass and rubber are insulators that hold charge; metals are conductors, so charge flows away through your hand.
adult: Ages 11 to 12. KS3 physics in England covers static electricity: charges separate when objects are rubbed together because electrons move, and charged objects exert forces on each other across a gap. Key words: electron, charge, positive, negative, neutral, attract, repel, insulator, conductor, discharge, spark.

Try it with a balloon and a wool jumper on a dry day. Hold the rubbed balloon near tiny bits of paper, then near a thin stream of water from a tap. Hang two rubbed balloons on threads and watch them push apart. Ask your child to say which way the electrons went each time.

Common mistakes: saying positive charges move (only electrons move in solids); saying rubbing makes charge (it only moves it, so the total stays the same); thinking like charges attract; thinking neutral objects feel no force; thinking you keep the charge after a spark; and thinking metals cannot be charged. A metal held in the hand does charge, but it conducts the charge away through the body.

In the lab your child drags a balloon across a jumper and watches four electrons move, names each charge, decides attract or repel for four pairs, lifts paper with a charged balloon (and sees an uncharged one fail), shuffles on a carpet to make two sparks, and sorts rubbed objects into insulators and conductors.

practice.prompt: A balloon rubbed on hair becomes negative. What happened?
choices: Electrons moved from the hair to the balloon
Positive charges moved from the balloon to the hair
practice.hint: Which charged particles are free to move in solids?
practice.explain: Electrons are the charges that move. The balloon gained electrons, so it is negative, and the hair lost them, so it is positive.

practice.prompt: Rubbing moves {a} electrons from a jumper to a balloon. How many extra electrons does the balloon have now?
practice.hint: Charge is not made or lost. Where did the jumper's electrons go?
practice.explain: Every electron the jumper lost went onto the balloon, so the balloon has {a} extra electrons and the jumper is missing {a}.

practice.prompt: A neutral jumper has {a} positive charges and {a} electrons. It loses {b} electrons to a balloon. How many more positive charges than electrons does it have now?
practice.hint: Its positive charges stay put. Count the electrons left and compare.
practice.explain: It still has {a} positive charges but only {=a-b} electrons, so it has {b} more positive than negative. It is positive.

practice.prompt: Two balloons have both been rubbed on the same jumper. What happens when they hang side by side?
practice.hint: Both gained electrons. What sign do they have?
practice.explain: Both are negative. Like charges repel, so they push apart, even across a gap.

practice.prompt: Why do you sometimes get a shock from a car door?
choices: Charge built up on you jumps to the metal as a spark
The car makes electricity in its door
practice.hint: What builds up on you as you slide across the seat?
practice.explain: Sliding moves electrons, so charge builds up on you. As your hand nears the metal, it jumps the gap as a spark and you become neutral.

pool.prompt: A charged comb pulls up tiny bits of uncharged paper. Why?
choices: It moves the paper's electrons, so the near side has the opposite charge
pool.hint: What does a negative comb do to the electrons in the paper?
pool.explain: The negative comb pushes the paper's electrons away. The near side is left positive, and unlike charges attract, so the paper is pulled up.

pool.prompt: A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positive. What happened to the silk?
choices: It gained electrons and became negative
It lost electrons and became positive
pool.hint: The electrons the glass lost had to go somewhere.
pool.explain: The glass lost electrons to the silk. The silk gained them, so it became negative by the same amount.

pool.prompt: A balloon has {a} extra electrons. You rub it again and {b} more move onto it. How many extra electrons does it have now?
pool.hint: Add the electrons from both rubs.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} extra electrons, so the balloon is more strongly negative.

pool.prompt: A positive rod is held near a negative balloon. What happens?
pool.hint: Are the charges the same or opposite?
pool.explain: Opposite (unlike) charges attract, so the balloon is pulled towards the rod.

pool.prompt: You rub a metal spoon while holding it, but it will not pick up paper. Why?
choices: Metal is a conductor, so the charge flows away through you
Rubbing never moves electrons in metals
pool.hint: What is different about how charge moves in metals?
pool.explain: Metals are conductors. Charge moves easily through them, so it flows through your hand to the ground instead of staying on the spoon.

pool.prompt: Shuffling on a carpet puts {a} extra electrons on you each step. After {b} steps you touch a metal handle and all the extra charge sparks across. How many electrons jump in the spark?
pool.hint: Work out how much charge built up first.
pool.explain: {a} electrons × {b} steps = {=a*b} electrons. The spark carries all {=a*b} to the metal, so you are neutral again.

pool.prompt: Which is true about rubbing a balloon on a jumper?
choices: New charge is made by the rubbing
Both end up with the same charge
pool.hint: Count the charges before and after.
pool.explain: Rubbing moves electrons from one object to the other. The total charge stays the same, and the two end up with opposite charges.

choices: A giant spark as built-up charge jumps through the air
Light from the Sun bouncing off clouds
Electrons being made inside the cloud
pool.hint: Think of a door-handle shock, much bigger.
pool.explain: Charge separates in a storm cloud. When enough builds up, it jumps through the air as a giant spark: lightning.

pool.prompt: Which material is best at holding a static charge?
pool.explain: Plastic is an insulator, so electrons rubbed onto it stay put. Copper and steel are conductors that let the charge flow away.

pool.prompt: A jumper loses 5 electrons to a balloon. What is the jumper's charge?
pool.hint: It kept all its positive charges but lost some negative ones.
pool.explain: With fewer electrons than positive charges, the jumper is positive. The balloon gained the 5 electrons, so it is negative.
